title: Navya Naveli Nanda Launches Naveli Ventures to Back India's Deep-Tech Ambitions
excerpt: The Nanda Family Office's venture arm will invest across deep-tech, space, AI, clean energy, advanced manufacturing and health — formalising a strategy three years in the making.
body:
• Navya Naveli Nanda formally launched Naveli Ventures on October 6, the venture arm of the Nanda Family Office, to back startups in deep-tech, space, clean energy, AI, advanced manufacturing and health.
  • The firm will invest through four routes — direct startup investments, commitments to institutional funds, co-investments, and academic and intellectual-property partnerships — and says it is not chasing quick returns.
  • No fund size, cheque range or portfolio has been disclosed. The LLP was actually registered in March 2023 with Navya and her brother Agastya Nanda as partners; this week was the formal unveiling of its strategy.
  • The launch rides a real wave: Indian deep-tech funding hit $2.1 billion across 289 deals in 2025, and the government's Rs 1 lakh crore R&D scheme plus a Rs 10,000 crore Fund of Funds 2.0 are pushing public money the same way.

Navya Naveli Nanda has formally unveiled Naveli Ventures, the venture arm of her family's office, with a mandate to back India's deep-tech and frontier-technology ambitions — the latest sign that Indian family offices are moving from passive wealth into research-led startup investing.

Nanda, the granddaughter of Amitabh Bachchan and managing partner of the firm, announced the launch in a LinkedIn post on October 6. Naveli Ventures will invest across six areas: deep-tech, space, clean energy, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and health. It will deploy through direct startup investments, commitments to institutional funds, co-investments, and partnerships with academic institutions and intellectual-property holders.

"We define ourselves not by sector but by the scale of the problem and the conviction of those solving it."

— Navya Naveli Nanda, Managing Partner, Naveli Ventures

Not actually new — now formal

The firm is not brand new. Naveli Ventures LLP was incorporated in March 2023, with Navya Nanda and her brother Agastya Nanda as designated partners. This week's announcement is the formal unveiling of an investment strategy that has been, by Nanda's own account, in development for some time. No fund size, cheque range, SEBI registration status or existing portfolio has been disclosed — a reminder that this is a strategy announcement, not a fund close.

https://x.com/YourStoryCo/status/2107748750366232994

The family office is associated with the Nanda business group, which includes Escorts Kubota, the farm and construction equipment manufacturer. Nanda recently completed the blended postgraduate programme for working professionals and entrepreneurs at IIM Ahmedabad. She said the family office's relationships across industry, government, academia and the investor community would be used to support the companies it backs.

Catching a real wave

The timing is deliberate. India is directing unprecedented public money toward commercially difficult technologies: the government's Research, Development and Innovation scheme carries a planned corpus of Rs 1 lakh crore over six years, with deep-tech, AI, biotech, energy transition and space as priority areas, and the Rs 10,000 crore Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0, notified in April, targets deep-tech and technology-led manufacturing.

Private capital is moving the same way. India Deep Tech Alliance data put deep-tech funding at $2.1 billion across 289 deals in 2025, lifting its share of Indian venture and private-equity activity to 15% from 4% in 2016, with AI funding up 58% to $1.22 billion. Recent closes include Capital-A's Rs 160 crore second fund, Bluehill.VC's Rs 400 crore frontier-tech fund, and a Rs 450 crore first close for the IIT Madras–Unicorn India Ventures frontier fund.

The family-office bet

Naveli Ventures fits a pattern: Indian family offices, sitting on generational industrial wealth, are increasingly writing cheques into research-led companies that traditional venture capital finds too slow or too capital-intensive. Nanda's pitch — "not chasing quick returns," problem-scale over sector, academic partnerships alongside startup bets — is the family-office value proposition in a sentence: patient capital with institutional doors already open.

The sceptic's view is equally plain. Family-office venture arms are easy to announce and hard to run; deep-tech returns take a decade; and without disclosed fund size or portfolio, Naveli Ventures is a promise, not yet a track record. The diaspora angle is real, though: Indian-origin founders in the US working on AI, space and clean energy have historically struggled to raise from Indian capital. If Naveli Ventures writes real cheques, it becomes one more bridge between Silicon Valley's Indian founders and Mumbai's family money.

What to watch

Watch for the first disclosed investments — their sectors and cheque sizes will reveal whether this is a serious deep-tech vehicle or a brand-building exercise. Also watch whether Naveli backs founders outside the family office's existing network, and whether it co-invests with the institutional funds now flooding Indian deep-tech. The strategy is sound; the execution is everything.
